Hello, and welcome to my 2025 Year in Review. This is something I would like to make a yearly occurrence, where I reflect on how my year went through the lens of the media I consumed. The hope here is to be a little more introspective with my downtime, and to start meaningfully identifying what it is I enjoy about certain things beyond a general sense of "it's good and I like how it makes me feel."

There was some unreasonable fear in my heart going into 2025, as I have a bad history with odd-numbered years. In 2019 I was screwed over by a university lecturer and had to waste my summer revisiting old coursework, in 2020 I got to skip the boring modules because nobody thought they were worth risking an outbreak. In 2021 I had to go back to uni for the modules deemed important, and in 2022 I finished my degree and got a job in the big city. In 2023 I had said job taken from me, and in 2024 I found a new job that continues to treat me well - treat me human. So with that pattern, I was wondering what 2025 would throw in my face; nothing, I'm glad to say.
br

Instead, I found myself rather blessed this year with fun new things popping up all over. I even found myself inspired to work on improving my game development skills, which we will hopefully see some tangible results for in 2026.

Picture the dreamer. Laying down, comfortably, the dreamer dreams in a manner familiar to both you and I - though with the singular exception that this is the dreamer's first dream. They have never known the grogginess of waking; the freedom of wakefulness; nor the relief of unawakening after a long day. All they know is a single story - the dream - which is told to them by the misfiring of neurons in their brain; it is equal parts unending and nonsensical.
Now, picture the dreamer dying.

In the only way they know how - in a dream - the dreamer dies a death as real as anything else they have known. Like the face of a loved one, the dream death is wrong - not a true death, nor an accurate facsimile - yet it is utterly real to the one  experiencing it. Writhing in somnambulistic pain, the thrashing body buckles to the demands of the mind. Demands to make the death real, to let the imagined pain end. Inevitably, the body in reality is subsumed by that which is dreamt. Slowly, but surely, the dreamer comes to a stop. Slowly, the dreamer experiences the inevitable - that which awaits us all at the end of our many dark tunnels.

Slowly, the dreamer's eyes flutter to wake. The pain fades, the imagined clots and scars and haemorrhages sublimate under the scrutiny of reality. The only life they have known fades away, and the dreamer throes with sudden derealization. The psyche maintains with nought but the promises of a life well lived - a death well had - and the end of a dream that they were to never see the other side of.

A caustic wailing fills the void. On it goes, until the dreamer is shocked still. A new sensation - their first wanting - a thirst. To know more starts, more ends, and perhaps more awakenings are they drawn to the quencher of all thirsts, the beginning of all lives: the ocean.

On the ocean, in a small - wooden - boat, atop a tall - churning - wave, the dreamer sees at sea what they can see see see. Their course vectors in on a new experience. Another wall of rocks. Over the years that they have now spent at sea, the dreamer has found the wall of rocks to be a singularly enthralling experience. Always able to put a smile on their face, and to put a new experience into the story of the world they live in. Eventually, the dreamer hoped, this particular genre of destination would be the one to close the door on the current chapter of their story - ideally opening a new one in the process. The dreamer and their decaying boat close in on what is sure to be another exciting venture in how far they can be flung up a crumbling rock face - when something stops them. A beam of light engulfs the floating termite nest.
"I see you." echoes from across the waves, revealing the source of the light. In these lifeless waters the dreamer finds themselves - for the very first time - not alone. The lighthouse speaks again.

"These paths you take, the places they lead you, are all known by me. They were once mine, and now I watch over them: the bed, the boat, the beach. This I do all for myself, but I will impose one thing unto you: a demand to your soul of the reason you come to be at sea."
A dreamer's new first,
A reply that will be their last;
"I don't want to be."

The dreamer's story is a fiction, but I'm sure it speaks to at least one non-fictitious human. One who lives Among Us and who has known the experience of a false reality shattering. If such a person truly can be said to exist (whatever that means) then I would suppose they rather enjoy the song 'Man Made of Meat' by the Viagra Boys. The irreverent exploration of what it means to exist as a human in the modern '20s is complimented by a catchy tune which creates a piece that is both easily digestible, yet horribly poetic to the intended audience. It is also the first song in what is now my favourite album, of which has made the V-Boys my favourite band. It is hard for me to imagine a person who does not enjoy at least one song on their quasi-self-titled album 'viagr aboys' (sic.) so give it a listen.

N.B. A personal recommendation for listening to the songs by the Viagra Boys that have an accompanying music video (which includes the opening trinity of viagr aboys!): listen to the audio; listen to it again whilst imagining a suitable music video; and finally watch whatever the fuck they decided would actually be a suitable music video. It's always a great time, and one that you can only ever experience once per track - which makes it just that extra bit special.

Hatsune Miku, the secret which hides in your WiFi. What could I, frayed ball of sinew and nerves that I am, possibly say about this worldwide phenomenon which the dear reader does not assuredly already know? Nothing, of course. Next paragraph.

Throughout this year, the semi-official Miku handler known to the wider public as DECO*27 has seen fit to drip-feed several new pieces which follow on from their late-2024 desecration of the idol's pure and perfect image. Starting at the already low bar of reimagining Miku as a jirai joshi, Deco has devolved her over the course of a year into some truly shocking things - culminating in a big scary face with a hole in it on a red (!!!) background.

The steady release schedule of the 'Dysfunctional Miku' series has added a comforting punctuation to 2025. With a pleasant variety of alternative designs for Ms. (please don't correct me on that) Hatsune, and two beautifully engaging music videos, each iteration has provided a solid memetic anchor for various points throughout the year. We have the year opening to "Monitoring", with a fresh faced miku knocking at our door - evoking the good natured start a year with some friendly first footing. Then we go to "Telepathy" which portrays a frazzled Miku infatuated with her summer love, slowly losing mental cohesion as the many responsibilities of a new year begin to claw away at her. Easing into autumn, the year lightens it's load and unfurls it's  bounty, and we see Miku start to frolic with potential with a chirpy little ditty before the winter's "Marshmallow" sees it all come crashing down with a metallic angst.

The songs are enjoyable, with some parts containing more emotion than I ever would have thought possible by an artist literally using someone else's voice, and the videos have captured the hearts of many more than just myself. Check out some of the remixes by various internet communities if you want to see Miku stretched into ever more untenable situations. Despite previously having never been a product I cared to consume, Hatsune Miku managed to become a part of my life in 2025. For that achievement alone, but also for keeping me grounded in time throughout the year, I would be amiss not to include it on this list. Though, if your only exposure to the blue-haired menace is the deeply cringe-worthy and oft creepy parts of the internet that she finds herself bound to, don't expect these to change your mind.

Hot and cold, a classic dichotomy, has existed since the forces of decay and stasis sought to bring forth reality. Hot and cold, the argument over one's preferred death via exposure, has existed since the realisation of an even more powerful force: human bickering. Personally I favour the cold. As an enzyme-based system, the merits of heat do not escape me - but they always seems to dissipate when push comes to shove. Conversely, when you find yourself at your lowest - be it physically, emotionally, or even financially - which primal force is it that comes knocking to check in?

When I describe something as 'cold', I often mean it as a term of endearment. Cold is reliable, heat makes things sloppy, a cube of ice is far more stable than a puddle of equivalent mass. For a person with as many loose frays as me, coldness is a necessity to maintain coherency. Thusly I have a special fondness for music that keeps my psyche somewhere desolate: "cold music". Man Made of Meat is the first song I would consider a 'favourite' which does not fall under this category, making it strange bedfellows with songs like Mili's 'world.execute(me)' and Battle Tapes' 'Talk Anymore'. The next song I present to you is my favourite piece of cold music that I listened to in 2025.

Futureproof is something of an outlier in the songs I have heard by Nothing but Thieves, but that makes me all the more glad to have finally stumbled over it. There may be some recency bias, as I first listened to it within about a week of writing this list, but this also puts it in the same time window for me as the next entry on this list - if you'll forgive the spoiler. Listening to Futureproof, a title which resonates somewhat thematically with SIGNALIS - my psyche is taken somewhere I can only otherwise see through the eyes of Elster. There is a raging desperation to the notes of the song, a deeply human pining for the destruction of entropy, and when you couple it with the struggles of a shattered construct seeking the only feelings it has ever known, it makes me want to cry. It makes me want to be able to cry. Perhaps, if I cry, then maybe I will feel as though I have become a better person.

Gaming
It is a wonderful thing, to be able to express yourself, and to instil an emotion within your audience.

It is rather straightforward for the medium of video games to make the audience think. No game exists without input, and no input exists without thought. However, for the medium to take that same, simple, cycle of stimulus becoming input becoming output and to turn it into an experience - one which forces the emotions of the character on to the player - requires a gifted mind. It might just require two.

Created by developer duo 'rose-engine,' SIGNALIS is a survival horror game - a genre I have explored relatively little of. Partly due to the relatively small market share of the genre, but primarily due to my cowardly aversion to anything labelled as 'horror.' Make no mistake, SIGNALIS has been labelled as exceptional by people far more genre savvy than myself. However, to put it in my own terms, if the average survival horror experience is even half as rich and engaging as SIGNALIS then I should find myself blessed to have an entire life's worth of backlog to backtrack and scavenge my way through.

It is quite possibly a surprise to hear this, given the genre, but I spent a relatively small percent of my time in SIGNALIS afraid. Nervous? Sure. Wrathful? When the moment suits it. Horny? We're all adults here. More than anything, however, I was enthralled by the sheer concentrated emotion that these moments conveyed, and the relative ease with which I was shifted between them. Many of these emotions, I have felt before both in media and in reality. No single thing, however, has made me feel emotions in the way SIGNALIS makes me feel them. Genuinely one of the best displays of the capabilities that video games have as an art form, and I would say an attack on SIGNALIS is simply a confession of somebody's inability to digest interactive media. It is as though rose-engine were gifted with a vision for the story they needed, to explore the ideas they wanted, and found the perfect gameplay to marriage the two together.

When you find yourself staring down a six foot amalgamation of steel, flesh, and hatred, with nothing but the clicking of a gun's hammer on an empty barrel to distract you from the wailing in your ear; when you find yourself measuring the value of your flesh against theirs; when the only thing keeping you going is the completely irrational desire to find the one with the white hair; that is when the game makes you feel it.
It is a terrible thing, to be capable of emotion, only to have it inflicted upon you so.
It is a game about love.

Continuing on, we have another game about love - one which also features a love interest with white hair, no less. Though given the lovingly monochromatic nature of Slay the Princess, it is possible we are supposed to imagine the Princess with whatever hair colour enamours us the most. Personally, I have found my soft spot for brunettes to have slowly been eroded this year - replaced by a fondness for silver wolves and wolvettes.

This game about love is, like most of it's ilk, a visual novel. Not usually my forte, as the usual examples of the genre that people recommend tend to exacerbate my least favourite parts of the medium: length, unimportant choices, and the inability to go through it whilst I sit on the toilet. Slay the Princess does not upend all of these elements, but 2 out of 3 is still a pass. Instead, it hones in on the unique strengths of the medium: encouraging the player to retread a story multiple times in a single session, and experiencing the branching effects of the decisions they make. It is the platonic ideal of a visual novel in my opinion.

The premise of the story is very easily digested, so I find myself dancing to try and balance recommending the game without spoiling everything. All I will leave you with is that everybody involved in presenting this story brought their A-game to create a little world that I find very enjoyable to dialogue my way through.

It takes a village to raise a child, everycunt kens that n aw these days, but what does it take to raise a village? Better yet, what does it take for a village to grow into a town? Whatever literal answer to this a town planner is liable to come up with, can probably be artistically reduced to mean "love." No this isn't another game about romance. It does have a Persona-esque feedback loop though of story into characters into gameplay into story, though, which is great. What isn't great about Persona, to me at least please don't bite, is the lack of characterisation in the setting. The cities always seem to take a back seat to the characters, but the two are inherently linked when you try and tell a story about systemic influences and the feedback loops they create. A niche gripe, but one which I can't help but bring up when talking about how great Promise Mascot Agency is. A game about breathing life into one of Japan's dying country towns, through the power of sentient brand Mascots that represent various aspects of Kaso-Machi's dwindling cultural and historical relevance. It is a game about what it takes to make a town.

In PMA, you control many of the actions taken by protagonist Michi on his way to try and graduate from a disgraced Yakuza legend into a reformed Yakuza legend - played by Takaya Kuroda, notable for also being the voice of Kiryu Kazuma. Along his blood-stained and oft wobbly path, you meet the remnants of the dying town Kaso-Machi - the few who remain - and it is through getting to know these few that the game both shows you the way forward and also explores the reasons these people (and sentient mascot costumes) both have for not leaving and for staking their lives on the potential rejuvenation of the town. One of these mascots is a Kappa who loves video games - he's played by Shuhei Yoshida, known for being the president of Sony Interactive Entertainment through 2008 to 2019. The gameplay largely consists of exploring Kaso-Machi in your suped-up Kei truck: going to specific places, gathering upgrades for your Mascot Agency, and generally tuning into the vibes that this environment creates. You also get given optional side objectives that involve helping the people of the town help the town bring in more people, and one of these characters is a crow mascot shrine caretaker - played by SWERY, known for being a designer on my favourite game ever (Tombi! 2: The Evil Swine Return.)

What I want to come across from this, from the name dropping, from the eccentric ways I have essentially described a giant fetch quest (with an excel spreadsheet tied in, that I'm not even mentioning) is that there is an immaculately curated feeling in this game. It's the perfect feeling for this game, one which brings people in from near and far and high and low and convinces them: that there is something special here, in Kaso-Machi, something worth putting your hat in the ring for and betting on. The spiritual main theme of the game ("Promises Lost, Promises Found" - available through all respectable media conglomerates) has been a mainstay in my morning alarm songs playlist, and every day that it is pseudorandomly chosen I wake up knowing that it's going to be a good day.
So come on down, to Kaso-Machi! There's even a white-haired love interest!

This year (2025), the year in which I am writing this paragraph (honest), is the year I learned to appreciate survival horror. Previously I stayed away from the genre, owing to it's closeness to horror and my closeness to pusillanimity, but I gave Sorry We're Closed a shot after it got high praise from fellow pretentious "video games are art" nerd Ben "Yahtzee" Croshaw. The current relevance of Yahtzee, and his handler group "Second Wind," to me and to the cultural space of 2025 is another story entirely - but Sorry We're Closed will be forevermore "the thing that got me into survival horror."

Sorry We're Closed is a game about love, in which the survival horror genre is used to explore the deeper meanings of what love means - all framed within the pursuit, or perhaps retreat, from a white-haired love interest who is oh no not again.

Please keep reading, otherwise these thoughts will die with me. Unlike every other game I've played which uses the love towards someone with white hair as a MacGuffin in a plot about love, Sorry We're Closed uses it more as a pretence with which to discuss the cost of love - change. In a world where angels and demons are real in a literal sense, you play as one of the few humans drawn into their world. Quickly you discover that angels can't stop falling in love with demons, demons can't stop falling in love with angels, and everybody wants a piece of you. So, the question floats overhead, how many pieces of yourself are you willing to give out in order to get what you think you want? Moreover, at what point do you start to fill in the gaps with little bits of other people? What are you, what are those around you, now that everybody has carved out chunks and played pick n' mix? Are they friends, foes, perhaps... lovers?

All these questions hopefully show you how well the game portrays the feeling of being the one lamb who knows that there is a way out of the abattoir, but not what it is. Keeping them vague hopefully compels you to experience it for itself, as the uniqueness of the story and setting really pulls it together and I would not wish to deprive you of that. Hopefully, more games will see that what makes a game beautiful or compelling is not visual or numerical value, not polygons nor subsurface samples, but that inimitable feeling from the hearts of the creators that could not be expressed in any other way.
Shoot for the heart, and love flows freely.

One of the most life-changing gaming experiences I have ever had was the decision to get good at a fighting game. After having not touched the genre before in my life, it allowed me to re-experience what it was like to learn a video game. They get a hard rap, fighting games, as being both difficult and hard to learn - but I have come to think that this consensus has been formed by people who have only seriously played one type of video game their whole life (usually shooters,  just as an observation) and who have long since forgotten the effort it first took them to figure out what the hell a video game even is. All video games are easy if you've only played however many variants of the same pattern for twenty years.

As an adult it's easy to only ever build upon your existing virtues, and never learn the base principles of a new field. Fighting games helped me break out of that rut, and in learning how to play them I also found how best to inject new concepts into my brain. There is no coincidence to me that after playing fighting games my life became richer: game development, 3D modelling, regular exercise, just to name a few things I have since taught myself. So when I say that fighting games are important to me, I am not talking simply about the technical aspects of the genre - but for the conceptual idea of the games therein and what they represent to me.

However, for the record, I do also have a particular appreciation for actual the mechanics and the gameplay of fighting games. The details of which I leave as an exercise to the reader, because words simply are not the right medium. Instead, the proper format with which to express how it feels to connect with another human being through melee is in vivo, it is it's own medium, and yes there is no substitute that sounds less stupid and/or pretentious.

So with that preamble complete, let me come at you with a disturbing twist: I hardly played any fighting games this year. Instead, my thirst for melee was quenched by the only game that I have ever fallen asleep during - football.

REMATCH was sold to me as a "football fighting game" (actually it was more sold as a comparison to Blue Lock, but we'll get to that.) The description intrigued me, as a team fighting game sounded like a horrible, incompatible, clash of themes and experiences. How can we peer into somebody's soul and impress ours unto it, if we share the pitch with 4-8 other players?

The solution to the dual-soul quandary is that REMATCH creates a temporary melding of minds. You intertwine with your teammates into an amalgamation of a football team, as do your opponents. In this, you are exposed to an average - a window into the heart of the zeitgeist. To bear the weight of your comrades sins, bare down on the hatred of the enemy team, and to triumph over it all in one glorious moment - where it all comes down to you, one amongst the throng, being the singular player to have "GOAL" attached to your name…
It turns grown adults into screaming facsimiles of Alan Partridge with disturbing ease.

Factorio stole the first half of spring from me this year. After first playing this game years ago, becoming mildly infatuated for a day or so, and then having any remaining love (and a decent portion of my critical thinking capacity) killed by a day-long charity gaming event - my opinion of Factorio has been somewhat collegial. While I stopped caring about it, there remains no denying - and in fact lots of praise worth giving to - the fact that Factorio is a meticulously crafted game; it contains hundreds, possibly even thousands, of hours of compelling, user-curated, gameplay; and it even has tremendous community engagement, even providing official modding support. The value proposition is clear, and the price infamously never waivers, so I thought it would make a good gift for a friend. Why not throw in the new Space Age DLC too? It's an official interpretation of a popular mod, made in conjunction with the original author, and has been getting pretty good reviews.

Starsector is one of the truest loves of my silly little life. It's a game about space ships, logistics, and market economies. The 'ins' of Starsector aren't relevant, but the 'outs' are a nebulous figure of man hours lost for me - somewhere in the hundreds. Each time I get a hankering for it, I wake up several weeks later with nothing new in my life save for an armada of designer flagships - and a growing itch for a game with even more granular logistics; one with, dare I even suggest… bespoke space ships?

After receiving an invitation from my friend, clearly satisfied with their gift, to come over and figure out some of the DLC-specific content together, I returned home and immediately got the DLC for myself and played Factorio for the first time in several years. It gets hazy after that, but apparently I have played Space Age for 155 hours now and my save file spans multiple planets; maintains a fully roboticised nuclear-grade military presence; and has an automated 'smart forge' capable of automatically reassembling itself to meet the needs of the supply network.
Once again I have taken a break from Factorio. Not out of apathy, this time, but fear.

In retrospect, Kingdom Come: Deliverance was probably a more important game for me than I ever gave it credit for at the time. Aside from the high quality gameplay mechanics - namely the combat system, which helped to prime me for my love of both technically demanding 1-on-1 melees and the concept of pushing a defensive button at the same time as your enemy pushing an offensive button. The story tells us of a young country bumpkin, too insignificant for me to bother naming, being forced by societal pressure into leaving his rote and slovenly life behind in favour of adventure and responsibilities (sword-fighting, learning to read, having to feed himself on a regular basis) in the big city. Coming to end on a cliffhanger - spoilers - we leave Henry at both the highest societal class and closest paternal relationship that he has ever known.

Needless to say, the implications for having fallen for this game in 2018 - a year where I travelled halfway across the world to go on a country-spanning road-trip with my semi-distant father, before returning home to attend university in Edinburgh - is not lost to me in hindsight. At the time, however, I remember admiring it primarily for: "being fun".
Oh, how my outlook has changed!

KCD accompanied me on many sleepless nights and joyless mornings, where I wrestled with being both a fish out of water and fucked in the head. Without Henry to provide a role model as a character who was going through parallel disturbances - even if at the time he was just the actuator of a "fun video game" to me - I cannot say with certainty if my head would have remained unexploded (metaphorically speaking) for the first, gruelling, year where I realised what life was really like when played as a character for whom I had spent eighteen years neglecting.
Now here we are, after: four years of university; one year of employment; one year of scornful unemployment; and one year of actually rewarding employment, approximately 7/8

of all the cells in my body have been refitted using proteins derived from food gained by my own efforts after leaving home - and Kingdom Come has arrived once more at the doors to my life. It has a sequel now. The sequel would like to meet uncle Connor.

Mechanically, every point has been stretched to an edge and sharpened to a blade. The combat system has had redundancies shaved, and now there is an additional

of parrying which involves pressing the

There's an ancestor of mine who I think of a lot. They were a simple spear holder, who lived and died in anonymity. I don't know their name, when they were alive, or how liable I am to really call them my ancestor, but it seems like such a historically common way to live that they're real enough to me. This ancestor spends a lot of time in my head - primarily since that's where they were born - when I play video games. I think about how they would react to and experience these virtual things: would they find an entirely new calling in these skeuomorphic pixels, or perhaps their unique ability to thrust a sharp stick through a shield wall would give them an edge in competitive shooters? It makes me a little sad, then, to know that they might have had a capacity for more joy in their lives than the technology available to them allowed.
When I play games that allow you to pilot a giant mechanical killing machine, a 'mech,' I feel a little jealous that they never had to knowingly miss out on their true calling.

There are two games I played this year which run strangely parallel to one another. Each was developed by From Software, despite not being in the Dark Souls series; each was played in great earnest by me, until an even greater imperative forced me to abandon them for several years; and I came back to both this year, completing them in the month of July.

The first game, much like Titanfall or the Lancer TTRPG, is another one of those times that I felt my soul click into place like a gear in a watch. Place me behind the cockpit of a giant machine, and years of dissociation wash out of me like piss in a swimming pool. It has to do with expression, I think, which is something I am generally rather poor at. From within my hollow, rotting, shell, my range of motions and capabilities have fairly well defined start and end points. There is only so much movement, and so many noises, that I can make to try and open up my soul to those around me - but that all goes out the window when you put me control of a mech. If I want to exit a situation by dashing hundreds of meters in a single second, I can, and if that requires me to put excess strain on a generator which is already barely containing a cataclysm-level event, I will show you just how important it is to me that this situation changes immediately by challenging that risk. It's why, I think, I still get transported back to the summer of '21 when I hear any of the songs I had on repeat whilst designing a Lancer campaign; it's one of those rare things that lets me feel like I exist.
That said, it should follow with reason that customisation is - in my opinion - the most important aspect of any 'mech game.' ARMORED CORE
TM
VI: FIRES OF RUBICON

allows you to create custom mechs which are composed of 4 weapon hardpoints, 4 chassis components, 3 system components, and a speciality module to boot. Each individual item in these slots will have at least 3 'main' stats associated with them, which balloon out to at least a dozen if you enable 'detailed view,' and each of these stats will have some form of impact on every other item in your composition. There is no mech, from my beloved Lancer or from my brain, that I have not been able to emulate in some form through this game. It is an excellent 'mech game,' and also contains one of the single best moments from any video game in probably the last decade. No spoilers, though, it's important to have an appetite for these things.

Chainsaw Man, a series which received it's first movie this year, is probably my favourite story across all forms of media I have consumed. Thanks to this movie's release, I am allowed to talk about the series within my self-imposed limits of 2025 CE - because the series has otherwise maintained an unwavering presence in my life since 2021.

The story of Chainsaw Man is effectively a subversion of the otherwise droll "shounen" genre which comes about by being the only frank example of what would happen if you took a young boy with nothing and gave him everything he needed - power, food, shelter - whilst yoking him with the chains of responsibility. Namely, he would turn into an annoying piece of shit who's only contribution to society comes about incidentally after first being manipulated by the only people with the power to grab his attention: babes.

If that sounds good to you, then I can easily recommend either the comic or animated formats of Chainsaw Man - and then the movie once you've reached the appropriate story beats. Also worth checking out, if you really are the fellow type of creature to find Denji's story engaging, is Tatsuki Fujimoto's other works. There are two connecting features of all of Fujimoto's works: a clear feeling that this is a strange Japanese man's only method of expressing himself, and a love for movies. Whether the entirety of 'Sayonara, Eri'; or the train fight from Fire Punch (the only time that I have ever pulled up a comic strip post-reading, in abstract, to show somebody else); I imagine that cinematography must have a pretty constant current flowing through Tatsuki's brain for it to appear so regularly in his static works.

That said, if you aren't interested in Chainsaw Man, feel free to skip the books. Feel free to skip the anime, too, but definitely still consider watching the movie. It's the closest we have to seeing this comic-centric film nerd actually making a motion picture, and it managed to make me feel an entirely new wave of emotions for a story I had already experienced.

There's a desperate, incompatible, web of hopes between every character in the Reze Arc that is slowly teased apart over the course of the film. From the voice acting, to the animation, to the sound design and music, every part shows a clear understanding for - whilst also expanding upon - the themes of one of the most consequential story beats of the Chain Saga. It must be an incredible way to experience it for the first time. For as seasoned a reader as myself though, I still felt incredibly impacted by it and was constantly taken aback by the details - new and old - that the movie throws in to compliment the existing story.

Perhaps this description makes me sound crazy, but maybe you're crazy too. Maybe we're the only two people in this abandoned cinema, shedding a tear for the same movie. If you want to see the movie for the first time, you gotta watch it. It's not in the comic book. Perhaps I make myself sound crazy.

A moment, please, to consider the future. Please contain yourself. Following a lifetime of apathy turned negativity (following the terrible events of 2023), I think that 2026 might be the year that I start to take a liking to football; or rather, if not next year - then never. A lot of pieces have come together this year to lay the groundwork for it. For example, the stunning performance of Scotland against Denmark for the world cup qualifiers with goals so bombastic they would not have looked out of place in REMATCH - my other soccer-adjacent love of this year. However, this line of thought will lead any astute reader (of which I would consider everybody who has sought this text out to be) to question: if these are what primed you for football, then what primed you for them?
Well, I'll give you a hint: it has nothing to do with football.

Written by Kaneshiro Muneyuki and illustrated by Nomura Yusuke, Blue Lock is a Japanese comic (you will hear me out loud admit to reading a 'manga' when you put a gun to my head) about a group of young men who all want to be become the world's greatest striker. This is NOT a story about football, I affirm, but is rather a surprisingly meditative exploration of both the nature of contest and the philosophy of competition. To this day, I still do not 'like' football, but I do 'love' Blue Lock - and judging by the intensity of both the artistry and prose that is plastered over the sport in their work, I would not be surprised if Muneyuki and Yusuke share these feelings. There is a passion, and an honesty, behind the emotions that they portray - using football as a backdrop - that will be familiar to anyone who has 'bet on' themselves before; if you've ever won or lost at something, you have had to reckon with the emotions that either of those evokes. It is how we handle these experiences, as a competitor in any field, that defines our growth. Blue Lock wields these emotions with razor sharp understanding, carving out a story and a heart all it's own, and uses it to create a story that is both invigorating and inspiring. If you can't find a plot beat relevant to yourself in Blue Lock, you haven't ever fought for something - and it could be the piece of media that inspires you to change that.
